narration: The Frog-Legged Court Craze
This is Canary dance. 16th–17th century.

Title card: Canary dance · Spain / France / Italy · 16th–17th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Rooted in the indigenous traditions of the Canary Islands, possibly related to the Tajaraste, the dance crossed to mainland Spain via enslaved people by 1552, where Diego Pisador noted it at funeral feasts.

By the late 16th and early 17th centuries, it captivated French, Italian, English, and Spanish courts, appearing in plays by William Shakespeare and dance manuals by Thoinot Arbeau (1589), Fabritio Caroso (1600), and Cesare Negri (1602).

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Initially functioning as a lively ballroom diversion or theatrical interlude within masques, the dance was framed around the dramaturgical theme of the 'sauvage' or indigenous wooing.
Spanish sources like Covarrubias noted its lineage from saltarello-style island dances, while contemporaries relished its bizarre, high-energy spectacle.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Choreographed primarily for a single couple, early versions featured rapid heel-and-toe stamps, deep jumps, and violent movements that earned it the nickname 'frogs legs.' Unlike rigid court steps of the galliarde, dancers engaged in free improvisation meant to mimic a playful 'savage' indigenous courtship.
By the 17th century in France, it incorporated elaborate cabrioles, turns, and battus in a fast ternary meter.
Watch for heel-and-toe stamp, frogs legs jump.

Captions name each signature move as it appears

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Early descriptions like Arbeau's noted simple meters, while Baroque interpretations embraced fast 3/4, 6/8, and dotted rhythms akin to a rapid gigue.
Girolamo Kapsberger wrote a famous 1640 virtuoso piece for chitarrone over a three-note basso ostinato, and Gaspar Sanz published a popular version for the Spanish baroque guitar in 1674.
Listen for the chitarrone, Spanish baroque guitar, strings/violin, lute.
The pulse is binary (early) or ternary 3/4, 6/8, 6/4 (Baroque).
A rapid, driving instrumental movement driven by sharp, short bow strokes or plucked strings, defined by an energetic dotted rhythm and an insistent repeating melodic or bass cell.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Dance masters Thoinot Arbeau, Fabritio Caroso, Cesare Negri, Livio Lupi da Caravaggio, and Juan de Esquivel Navarro documented its steps.
Baroque composers including Girolamo Kapsberger, Gaspar Sanz, J.S. Bach, Henry Purcell, and Jean-Baptiste Lully cemented its rhythmic profile.

Manifested across Europe with distinct local flavors: Spanish guitar adaptations (Gaspar Sanz), Italian theatrical balletto sequences (Negri, Caroso), and refined French baroque variations emphasizing brilliant footwork and rapid tempos.
Rooted in Canary Islands indigenous movement traditions (such as the Tajaraste), influencing Baroque suite movements and sharing structural affinities with the gigue and saltarello.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Canary dance is variant of gigue: Often compared to the gigue, though considered faster and sharper in execution.
Canary dance is variant of saltarello: Covarrubias described the Canary dance as a type of saltarello originating from the Canary Islands.
